context: Current closing price of Amazon (AMZN): $266.32 USD as of 2026-05-25.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the current price level, anchored around 267–272 across the three horizons. At the one-day horizon, I expected very little movement, so the estimate of 267.5 essentially represents near-term mean reversion with minimal directional bias. At one week, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 269, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with typical equity index behavior over short holding periods. At one month, the estimate of 272 continues that gradual upward trend, incorporating the historical tendency of broad equity indices to drift higher over time when no strong bearish catalyst is immediately apparent. In all three cases, the point estimates are not a strong directional call but rather a baseline extrapolation from recent price levels with a small positive drift baked in.

The confidence interval widths reflect standard scaling of uncertainty with time. At one day, the 90% interval of 258–277 spans roughly 19 points, consistent with typical daily volatility for an index in this price range, implying an annualized volatility assumption in the moderate range. At one week, the interval widens to 36 points (251–287), reflecting the square-root-of-time scaling that dominates short-horizon uncertainty. At one month, the interval expands further to 70 points (238–308), capturing the compounding of daily fluctuations over roughly 21 trading days. The widths were also informed by the general macro environment, including sensitivity to interest rate expectations, earnings season timing, and geopolitical backdrop, all of which add fat-tail risk beyond pure statistical volatility estimates.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a sharply worse-than-expected jobs report, a renewed inflation surprise prompting aggressive Federal Reserve communication, or an unexpected credit event in financial markets — could easily push prices below the lower bound of the one-month interval. Geopolitical escalation or a liquidity shock could also produce sharp moves that exceed the historical volatility assumptions embedded in my intervals. On the upside, an unexpectedly strong earnings season, a dovish pivot signal from central banks, or a resolution of ongoing geopolitical tensions could drive prices above 308 within a month. These tail events are by construction not fully captured in a 90% confidence interval, meaning roughly one in ten outcomes should be expected to fall outside these bounds even under normal conditions, and in stressed market environments that fraction could be considerably higher.
